## Company: Nickel Asia Corporation (NIKL)
Sector: Mining and Oil / Mining
Nickel Asia Corporation (NIKL) was incorporated on July 24, 2008 with the Securities and Exchange Commission primarily to engage in the business of mining of all kinds of ore, metals, and minerals and in the business of generation, transmission, distribution and supply of electricity to cities and other localities.

The Company owns six mines operated by its subsidiaries: the Rio Tuba mine in Palawan operated by Rio Tuba Nickel Mining Corporation; the Taganito mine in Surigao del Norte operated by Taganito Mining Corporation; the Tagana-an mine in Surigao del Norte and Manicani mine in Eastern Samar operated by Hinatuan Mining Corporation; the Cagdianao mine in Dinagat Islands operated by Cagdianao Mining Corporation; and the Dinapigue mine in Isabela operated by Dinapigue Mining Corporation.

NIKL has other properties in various stages of exploration for nickel, while continuing to seek opportunities in copper and gold. The Company also exports saprolite and limonite ore to customers in Japan and China.

NIKL's other subsidiaries include Samar Nickel Mining Resources Corporation; Coral Pearl Developments Limited; CDTN Services Company, Inc.; and Emerging Power, Inc.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
Nickel Asia Corporation is a straightforward business to understand — it mines and exports nickel ore (saprolite and limonite) from six Philippine mines, primarily selling to Japanese and Chinese customers. The company is the dominant player in Philippine nickel production, which makes its operations legible. Its newer Emerging Power subsidiary and the Shell JV developing 240 MWp of solar add complexity, but these are intelligible businesses in their own right. The diversification into renewables is modest relative to the core mining operation, so the circle of competence question reduces to: can you forecast nickel supply and demand over a decade? That is genuinely hard, which is itself a meaningful caution.

The moat question is where the thesis buckles. Nickel is a commodity, and commodity producers are price takers — there is no brand, no switching cost, no network effect shielding NIKL's margins when ore prices fall. NIKL's scale and its portfolio of MPSA-licensed reserves constitute a real asset base, but not a durable competitive advantage in the Rule #1 sense. Worse, the structural backdrop is deteriorating: Indonesia's HPAL processing capacity is on track to nearly double by end of 2026, driving a global nickel surplus projected at 288,000 tonnes that year. Simultaneously, Chinese EV manufacturers are accelerating their shift from nickel-heavy NMC chemistries to lithium iron phosphate batteries, undermining the demand narrative that underpinned nickel's bull case. NIKL's own analysts project earnings declining from approximately ₱4.2 billion today to ₱3.4 billion by 2028 as margin compression sets in — a telling admission from the bull camp.

Management earns credit for discipline: debt-to-equity of 0.25x signals conservative capital allocation, the SBTi net-zero validation and Fortune SEA 500 recognition suggest a well-run operation, and the March 2025 MOU to explore a Philippine nickel processing plant shows forward-looking thinking about moving up the value chain. The ore export ban risk — which briefly threatened NIKL's entire revenue model when the Senate passed such a bill in February 2025 — was ultimately removed from the final legislation, a relief. Still, the regulatory environment for Philippine mining remains politically charged, and Amnesty International flagged concerns over community consultation processes at approved NIKL projects in early 2025. No smoking gun, but worth monitoring.

Valuation is the clearest strike against entry. At ₱4.54, NIKL trades below its Rule #1 sticker price of ₱4.25 — meaning the current price already implies the full fair value of its earnings at the assumed growth rate. The 50% margin-of-safety buy price is ₱2.12, and the stock trades at more than double that level. Even using analyst consensus targets of ₱5.18–₱5.53, the upside is thin relative to the commodity cycle risk embedded in the position. With nickel prices expected to hover in the $15,000–$16,500/tonne range through 2026 amid persistent oversupply, there is no near-term catalyst to re-rate earnings upward. A 4% dividend yield provides some consolation but does not compensate for downside if ore prices slide further or if the export ban debate resurfaces.

NIKL is a well-managed, financially conservative business in a structurally difficult commodity with no durable moat and an entry price offering zero margin of safety. The business quality is respectable, but Rule #1 demands both quality and price — and the price here asks you to pay fair value for a company facing multi-year earnings headwinds from Indonesian oversupply and shifting EV battery chemistry. Pass at ₱4.54. The watch price would be closer to ₱2.50–₱3.00, where the dividend yield would be more meaningful and the margin of safety more credible. If nickel prices decline enough to push the stock into that range, revisit with updated earnings estimates.
